title: The town that moved
text: Kiruna exists because of iron, and iron now {{1}} it to move. The Swedish arctic town grew around the world's largest underground iron mine, and for a century the miners simply dug underneath the streets. But the {{2}} worked inward, and by 2004 geologists warned that deformation would reach the town centre; entire districts began to {{3}} several centimetres a year. The solution was {{4}}: move the town. Over two decades, Sweden is {{5}} thousands of buildings — the church, weighing 672 tonnes, was winched whole onto trailers and rolled two kilometres to its new foundations, watched by crowds and live television. Streets, pipes and the clock tower {{6}} them; residents were compensated at twenty-five per cent above market value, and heritage buildings were {{7}} rather than demolished. Not everything moved, of course: the oldest quarters, with their cheapest rents and their histories, became {{8}} ground. Kiruna is the rare town that gets to plan its own disappearance — a rehearsal, some suggest, for the relocations that climate change will force on less willing places.

gaps.explanation: 'iron now compels it to move' — leaves it no choice; expel = force out, repel = drive back.
'the excavation worked inward' — the mining of the ground; exclamation = a cry or remark.
'districts began to subside' — sink as the ground below is removed; submerge = go underwater, subsidise = pay part of the cost.
'the solution was drastic: move the town' — radical and extreme; droll = amusingly odd.
'Sweden is relocating thousands of buildings' — moving them to new sites; retrieve = get back.
'the clock tower followed them' — came along afterwards; foil = thwart.
'heritage buildings were salvaged rather than demolished' — rescued and kept; savage = attack ferociously.
'became surrendered ground' — given up to the mine; surmount = overcome.
